course.title: Latin American History
course.description: A survey of Latin American history from the great pre-Columbian civilizations through conquest, colonial rule, independence, and the modern era. Across ten lessons you will trace the Maya, Aztec, and Inca worlds, the Columbian Exchange, the Atlantic slave trade, the wars of liberation, and the upheavals of the twentieth century. Structure and facts adapted from Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia (CC BY-SA 4.0).

questions.prompt: The capital of the Aztec (Mexica) empire, built on an island in Lake Texcoco, was…
questions.explanation: Tenochtitlan, founded around 1325, sat on an island in Lake Texcoco; its ruins lie under modern Mexico City.

questions.prompt: In what year did Christopher Columbus first reach the Caribbean under the sponsorship of Castile?
questions.explanation: Columbus made landfall in the Bahamas in October 1492 on the first of four voyages.

questions.prompt: The Inca empire, the largest in the pre-Columbian Americas, was centered on which highland city?
questions.explanation: Cuzco, in the Peruvian Andes, was the heart of Tawantinsuyu, the Inca realm.

questions.prompt: The transfer of crops, animals, people, and diseases between the Americas and the rest of the world is called the…
questions.explanation: The Columbian Exchange moved maize and potatoes east and wheat, horses, and smallpox west.

questions.prompt: Which leader is remembered as 'El Libertador' for his campaigns across northern South America?
questions.explanation: Simon Bolivar led independence fights in Venezuela, Colombia, Ecuador, Peru, and Bolivia.

questions.prompt: The Mexican Revolution broke out in which year against the long rule of Porfirio Diaz?
questions.explanation: The revolution began in 1910 and reshaped Mexico through the 1917 Constitution.

questions.prompt: The Cuban Revolution brought which leader to power in January 1959?
questions.explanation: Fidel Castro's movement overthrew Fulgencio Batista on January 1, 1959.

questions.prompt: Brazil was the last country in the Americas to abolish slavery, which it did in…
questions.explanation: The Lei Aurea (Golden Law) ended slavery in Brazil in 1888.

lessons.title: Pre-Columbian civilizations: Maya, Aztec, Inca
lessons.grammar_note: Dates before the common era count down (1200 BCE is older than 400 BCE); dates in the common era count up (900 CE is older than 1500 CE).

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Name the three best-known civilizations of the Americas before European contact, place each in its region and time, and describe one lasting achievement of each. Warm-up: from the diagnostic, which city sat on an island in a lake, and which empire was centered on Cuzco? By the end you should be able to explain why these were sophisticated states, not isolated villages, and to resist the old myth that the Americas were 'empty' before 1492. The peoples discussed here were the ancestors of many communities living across Latin America today, and their descendants still speak Maya, Nahuatl, Quechua, and Aymara.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Long before Europeans arrived, the Americas held dense populations and complex societies. In Mesoamerica, the Olmec (about 1200 to 400 BCE) and the great city of Teotihuacan (roughly 100 BCE to 550 CE) set patterns later cultures built on. The Maya flourished in the Yucatan and Central America, especially during their Classic period from about 250 to 900 CE, organized as competing city-states rather than one empire. The Mexica, usually called the Aztecs, rose in central Mexico in the fifteenth century. In the Andes, the Inca forged the largest state in the hemisphere during the 1400s. Each developed farming suited to its land, monumental architecture, record-keeping, and organized religion, supporting millions of people.

sections.heading: Key events and figures
sections.text: The Maya built cities such as Tikal, Palenque, and Copan, created a full writing system of hieroglyphs, tracked the heavens, and used a place-value mathematics that included a symbol for zero; their southern lowland centers declined around the ninth century. The Mexica founded Tenochtitlan about 1325 and, through the Triple Alliance of 1428 with Texcoco and Tlacopan, dominated central Mexico; they farmed floating garden plots called chinampas and spoke Nahuatl. The Inca state, Tawantinsuyu, expanded rapidly after about 1438 under the ruler Pachacuti, linking its territory with thousands of miles of roads, keeping accounts on knotted cords called quipu, and building sites such as Machu Picchu. By 1500 the Inca realm may have held ten million or more people.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) Which civilization used a writing system of hieroglyphs and a symbol for zero? 2) What was the Mexica capital, and about when was it founded? 3) Name the alliance of 1428 that made the Mexica dominant. 4) What were quipu used for? 5) Under which ruler did the Inca expand rapidly after about 1438? 6) What farming method did the Mexica use in the lake? Answers: 1) the Maya. 2) Tenochtitlan, founded about 1325. 3) the Triple Alliance (with Texcoco and Tlacopan). 4) keeping records and accounts on knotted cords. 5) Pachacuti. 6) chinampas, floating garden plots built up from the lakebed.

sections.heading: Common mistakes and exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: treating 'Aztec' and 'Maya' as the same people; they lived in different regions and peak eras, the Maya earlier and farther southeast, the Mexica later and in central Mexico. Mistake: assuming the Inca had writing like the Maya; the Inca recorded information on quipu instead. Mistake: imagining a thinly settled land, when in fact tens of millions of people lived across the Americas in 1500. Exit: (a) In which modern country was the Inca capital, Cuzco? (b) During which centuries was the Maya Classic period? Answers: Peru; roughly 250 to 900 CE.

lessons.title: The European conquest and the Columbian Exchange
lessons.grammar_note: Conquest was not a single event but decades of campaigns; disease, Indigenous alliances, and internal divisions mattered as much as weapons.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Explain how small European expeditions toppled two large empires within a few decades, and describe the Columbian Exchange and its enormous human cost. Warm-up: in what year did Columbus first reach the Caribbean, and which two Indigenous empires fell to Spanish-led forces? You should finish able to say why disease and local alliances, not muskets alone, decided these conquests, and to speak about the resulting loss of Indigenous life with the seriousness it deserves. The conquest reshaped the Americas permanently, but it met determined resistance and relied heavily on Indigenous allies and labor.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: After 1492 Spain and Portugal claimed vast American territories, divided between them by the 1494 Treaty of Tordesillas. Spanish expeditions led by a few hundred men overturned the Mexica and Inca states, but they could not have done so alone. Epidemic diseases brought from the Old World, above all smallpox, swept through populations with no prior exposure and killed enormous numbers, in some regions as much as ninety percent over the century that followed. Conquistadors also exploited rivalries, recruiting peoples who resented Mexica or Inca rule. The historian Alfred Crosby named the two-way transfer of life across the Atlantic the Columbian Exchange, a process that remade diets and landscapes worldwide.

sections.heading: Key events and figures
sections.text: Hernan Cortes landed in Mexico in 1519, allied with the Tlaxcalans and others, and with his interpreter Malintzin reached the court of Moctezuma II; after fierce fighting and a smallpox outbreak, Tenochtitlan fell in August 1521. Francisco Pizarro reached Peru as the Inca were weakened by a civil war between the brothers Atahualpa and Huascar; he seized Atahualpa at Cajamarca in 1532 and had him executed in 1533, taking Cuzco the same year. The Columbian Exchange carried maize, potatoes, tomatoes, cacao, and tobacco to the Old World, and brought wheat, sugar, horses, cattle, and pigs, along with devastating diseases, to the Americas.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) Which treaty of 1494 divided the Americas between Spain and Portugal? 2) Who led the campaign against the Mexica, and in what year did Tenochtitlan fall? 3) What internal conflict had weakened the Inca before Pizarro arrived? 4) Name two crops that traveled from the Americas to the Old World. 5) What disease most devastated Indigenous populations? 6) Who coined the term 'Columbian Exchange'? Answers: 1) the Treaty of Tordesillas. 2) Hernan Cortes; Tenochtitlan fell in 1521. 3) a civil war between Atahualpa and Huascar. 4) any two of maize, potatoes, tomatoes, cacao, tobacco. 5) smallpox. 6) Alfred Crosby.

sections.heading: Common mistakes and exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: crediting the conquest to superior weapons alone, when disease and large Indigenous alliances were decisive. Mistake: picturing Indigenous peoples as passive, when many fought the invaders for years and others shaped events as allies, interpreters, and leaders. Mistake: treating the population collapse as a minor side note rather than one of the greatest demographic catastrophes in history. Exit: (a) Which disease caused the most deaths? (b) Which empire did Pizarro overthrow, and roughly when? Answers: smallpox; the Inca empire, in the early 1530s.

lessons.title: The colonial era: viceroyalties, encomienda, casta, and Church
lessons.grammar_note: Keep the labor systems straight: the encomienda granted tribute and labor to a colonist; the mita was a rotational Andean labor draft used in the mines.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Describe how Spain governed its American territories, the labor systems that extracted wealth and Indigenous labor, the racial hierarchy of the casta system, and the central role of the Catholic Church. Warm-up: which two early viceroyalties do you think Spain created first, and around which cities? By the end you should be able to connect silver mining, forced labor, and the social order into one picture of colonial society, and to recognize that this order rested on coercion while also producing new peoples, languages, and faiths that endure today.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Spain ruled through viceroyalties, large administrative units headed by a viceroy answering to the crown. New Spain was organized in 1535 with its capital at Mexico City, and Peru in 1542 with its capital at Lima; two more, New Granada and the Rio de la Plata, were added in the eighteenth century. Colonists extracted labor and tribute first through the encomienda, a grant of Indigenous workers, and later through the repartimiento and the Andean mita. Silver from Potosi, discovered in 1545, and from Zacatecas financed a global trade reaching as far as Manila. A hierarchy of ancestry, the casta system, ranked people by descent.

sections.heading: Key events and figures
sections.text: The friar Bartolome de las Casas denounced the abuse of Indigenous people and helped push the crown to issue the New Laws of 1542, which limited the encomienda, though enforcement was weak. The casta system placed Spanish-born peninsulares and American-born criollos at the top, with mestizos, mulattoes, Indigenous peoples, and Africans ranked below, shaping law and opportunity. The Church evangelized through missionary orders, the Franciscans, Dominicans, and Jesuits, and through the apparition of the Virgin of Guadalupe reported in 1531, which became central to Mexican devotion. The Jesuits ran reductions, protected mission communities in Paraguay, until the crown expelled the order from its empire in 1767.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) Name the first two viceroyalties and their capitals. 2) What did the encomienda grant to a colonist? 3) Which silver city, opened in 1545, anchored the colonial economy? 4) Who were the peninsulares? 5) Which friar campaigned against the abuse of Indigenous people? 6) In what year were the Jesuits expelled from the Spanish empire? Answers: 1) New Spain (Mexico City) and Peru (Lima). 2) Indigenous labor and tribute. 3) Potosi. 4) Spanish-born colonists, at the top of the casta hierarchy. 5) Bartolome de las Casas. 6) 1767.

sections.heading: Common mistakes and exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: confusing the encomienda with land ownership; it was a grant of people's labor and tribute, not of the land itself. Mistake: treating the casta system as neutral description rather than a hierarchy that assigned rights by ancestry. Mistake: assuming conversion erased Indigenous belief, when in practice Catholic and Indigenous traditions often blended. Exit: (a) Which rotational labor draft supplied the Andean silver mines? (b) Which 1542 reform tried to curb the encomienda? Answers: the mita; the New Laws.

lessons.title: The Atlantic slave trade and plantation economies
lessons.grammar_note: Abolition came at very different dates: Haiti freed itself by 1804, the British Caribbean by 1838, Cuba in 1886, and Brazil last, in 1888.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Describe the scale of the transatlantic slave trade, the plantation economies it fed, the resistance of enslaved people, and the long road to abolition. Warm-up: which American country received the largest number of enslaved Africans, and which was the last to end slavery? You should finish able to state the trade's dimensions honestly, to name the Haitian Revolution as a landmark of emancipation, and to recognize that enslaved and freed Africans and their descendants were central builders of Latin American societies and cultures, not a footnote to them.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Over roughly four centuries, some twelve and a half million Africans were forced onto ships bound for the Americas, of whom about ten and a half million survived the Middle Passage. Brazil received by far the most, several million people, and the Caribbean nearly as many across its islands. Their forced labor powered plantation economies built first on sugar, in northeastern Brazil and the Caribbean, and later on coffee and other crops. Enslaved people resisted constantly, through daily defiance, flight, and revolt, and built free communities such as the quilombo of Palmares in Brazil and maroon settlements elsewhere. Slavery shaped the region's demography, religion, music, and cuisine.

sections.heading: Key events and figures
sections.text: Sugar estates in Pernambuco and Bahia made Brazil an early plantation powerhouse, and the Caribbean islands followed. The most dramatic act of resistance was the Haitian Revolution of 1791 to 1804, in which enslaved people in the French colony of Saint-Domingue, led in turn by Toussaint Louverture and Jean-Jacques Dessalines, overthrew slavery and colonial rule to found Haiti in 1804, the first nation born of a successful slave revolt. Abolition elsewhere came gradually: Britain ended slavery in its colonies between 1833 and 1838, Cuba abolished it in 1886, and Brazil last of all with the Lei Aurea of 1888.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) About how many Africans were embarked on the transatlantic trade? 2) Which American country received the most enslaved people? 3) What crop first drove the plantation economy? 4) What was Palmares? 5) When did the Haitian Revolution begin and end? 6) In what year did Brazil abolish slavery? Answers: 1) roughly twelve and a half million. 2) Brazil. 3) sugar. 4) a large free community (quilombo) of escaped enslaved people in Brazil. 5) 1791 to 1804. 6) 1888.

sections.heading: Common mistakes and exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: thinking enslaved people accepted their condition; resistance ranged from everyday acts to the full revolution in Haiti. Mistake: assuming all countries abolished slavery at once, when the dates span more than half a century. Mistake: overlooking the central African contribution to Latin American religion, music, and food. Exit: (a) Which country became the first independent nation born of a slave revolt, and when? (b) Which was the last country in the Americas to abolish slavery? Answers: Haiti, in 1804; Brazil, in 1888.

questions.prompt: The Triple Alliance of 1428 that made the Mexica dominant joined Tenochtitlan with…
questions.explanation: Tenochtitlan, Texcoco, and Tlacopan formed the alliance that dominated central Mexico.

questions.prompt: Tenochtitlan fell to Cortes and his Indigenous allies in which year?
questions.explanation: After a siege and a smallpox outbreak, the Mexica capital fell in August 1521.

questions.prompt: Which of these traveled from the Americas to the Old World in the Columbian Exchange?
questions.explanation: Potatoes, maize, tomatoes, cacao, and tobacco went east; wheat, horses, and cattle came west.

questions.prompt: The first two Spanish viceroyalties, New Spain and Peru, had their capitals at…
questions.explanation: New Spain was governed from Mexico City (1535) and Peru from Lima (1542).

questions.prompt: The colonial grant of Indigenous labor and tribute to a Spanish colonist was called the…
questions.explanation: The encomienda granted a colonist the labor and tribute of Indigenous people.

questions.prompt: The Haitian Revolution produced the Americas' first nation born of a slave revolt in which year?
questions.explanation: Haiti declared independence in 1804 after enslaved people overthrew French rule.

lessons.title: The independence movements
lessons.grammar_note: Two great campaigns converged: Bolivar's drove south from the north, San Martin's north from the south, meeting in Peru around 1822.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Explain why most of Latin America won independence in the two decades after 1808, and identify the main leaders and turning points in Spanish South America, Mexico, and Brazil. Warm-up: which leader is called 'El Libertador', and which other general liberated the far south? By the end you should be able to connect the crisis in Spain to the creole revolts it unleashed, to tell the northern and southern South American campaigns apart, and to see why Brazil's path differed from the rest. These were hard-fought wars, not sudden gifts, and they left new nations to be built.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: The spark was European: in 1808 Napoleon invaded Spain and deposed King Ferdinand VII, throwing imperial authority into doubt. American-born elites, the creoles, long resentful of exclusion by peninsulares and inspired by Enlightenment and revolutionary examples, seized the opening. In Spanish South America two great liberation campaigns converged. Simon Bolivar drove south from Venezuela and New Granada, while Jose de San Martin pushed north from the Rio de la Plata, crossing the Andes to free Chile and then Peru. Mexico's struggle began as a popular uprising and ended in a conservative compromise. Brazil, by contrast, separated from Portugal almost peacefully.

sections.heading: Key events and figures
sections.text: Bolivar won decisive victories at Boyaca in 1819, Carabobo in 1821, and Pichincha in 1822, forging the union of Gran Colombia. San Martin led the declaration of Argentine independence at Tucuman in 1816, crossed the Andes with Bernardo O'Higgins to win Chacabuco in 1817 and Maipu in 1818, and proclaimed Peru's independence in 1821; the two leaders met at Guayaquil in 1822. The Battle of Ayacucho in 1824 sealed Spain's defeat in South America. In Mexico, Miguel Hidalgo's Grito de Dolores of September 16, 1810, began the fight, completed under Agustin de Iturbide in 1821. In Brazil, Dom Pedro declared independence in 1822.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) What European event of 1808 triggered the independence crisis? 2) Who were the creoles? 3) Which general crossed the Andes to liberate Chile and Peru? 4) Name Bolivar's victory of 1821 in Venezuela. 5) Whose Grito de Dolores began Mexico's struggle, and when? 6) Who declared Brazil's independence, and in what year? Answers: 1) Napoleon's invasion of Spain and the deposing of Ferdinand VII. 2) American-born people of Spanish descent. 3) Jose de San Martin. 4) Carabobo. 5) Miguel Hidalgo, on September 16, 1810. 6) Dom Pedro, in 1822.

sections.heading: Common mistakes and exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: thinking independence was granted peacefully everywhere; most of Spanish America won it through years of war. Mistake: mixing up the two campaigns, when Bolivar worked in the north and San Martin in the south before they met in Peru. Mistake: assuming Mexico and Brazil followed the same path, when Mexico's began as a popular revolt and Brazil's came through its own prince. Exit: (a) Which 1824 battle sealed Spain's defeat in South America? (b) Where did Bolivar and San Martin meet in 1822? Answers: the Battle of Ayacucho; Guayaquil.

lessons.title: The nineteenth century: caudillos and nation-building
lessons.grammar_note: A caudillo was a personalist strongman whose authority rested on loyalty and force more than on stable institutions.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Explain why the new republics struggled to build stable states after independence, identify the caudillos and the liberal-conservative conflicts of the era, and describe the export economies and the major wars that redrew borders. Warm-up: why might winning a war of independence be easier than governing the country afterward? By the end you should be able to connect weak institutions, regional power, and economic dependence on exports, and to see how several nineteenth-century wars reshaped the map of the region before the century closed.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Independence left fragile states with contested borders and thin institutions. Large unions broke apart: Gran Colombia dissolved in 1830 into Venezuela, Ecuador, and New Granada, and the United Provinces of Central America came apart by the early 1840s. Power often fell to caudillos, strongmen whose rule rested on personal loyalty and armed force. Politics divided liberals, who favored free trade, limits on the Church, and federalism, against conservatives, who defended tradition, Church privileges, and central authority. Economically, the republics leaned on exporting raw materials, guano, nitrates, coffee, beef, and wheat, drawing heavy British investment and tying their fortunes to world prices.

sections.heading: Key events and figures
sections.text: Caudillos such as Juan Manuel de Rosas in Argentina and Antonio Lopez de Santa Anna in Mexico dominated politics for decades. In Mexico, the liberal reform led by Benito Juarez produced the Laws of Reform in the 1850s, followed by the French intervention that installed Maximilian from 1862 until his fall in 1867. The United States took roughly half of Mexico's territory in the war of 1846 to 1848, closed by the Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo. The War of the Triple Alliance from 1864 to 1870 devastated Paraguay, and the War of the Pacific from 1879 to 1883 left Bolivia landlocked after defeat by Chile. Brazil remained a monarchy until it became a republic in 1889.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) What is a caudillo? 2) Into which three states did Gran Colombia dissolve in 1830? 3) Which Mexican liberal led the mid-century Reform? 4) Which treaty ended the Mexican-American War? 5) Which war left Bolivia without a coastline? 6) In what year did Brazil become a republic? Answers: 1) a personalist strongman ruling through loyalty and force. 2) Venezuela, Ecuador, and New Granada. 3) Benito Juarez. 4) the Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo (1848). 5) the War of the Pacific (1879 to 1883). 6) 1889.

sections.heading: Common mistakes and exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: assuming independence brought immediate stability, when most republics faced coups, civil wars, and shifting borders for decades. Mistake: treating liberals and conservatives as modern party labels rather than nineteenth-century camps split over trade, the Church, and central power. Mistake: forgetting that export dependence left economies exposed to world price swings. Exit: (a) Which 1864 to 1870 war devastated Paraguay? (b) Who installed Maximilian in Mexico, and until what year did he rule? Answers: the War of the Triple Alliance; France, until 1867.

lessons.title: Twentieth-century revolutions and dictatorships
lessons.grammar_note: During the Cold War, local conflicts were often read through a global contest between the United States and the Soviet Union, which shaped outside intervention.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Describe the Mexican and Cuban revolutions, explain how the Cold War shaped the region, and identify the military dictatorships of the later twentieth century and the return to democracy. Warm-up: in what year did the Mexican Revolution begin, and who came to power in Cuba in 1959? By the end you should be able to connect demands for land and sovereignty to revolution, to see how superpower rivalry drew in Latin America, and to speak carefully about the human cost of the dictatorships, including the thousands who were killed or forcibly disappeared.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: The century opened with the Mexican Revolution of 1910 to 1920, a violent, many-sided struggle against the long rule of Porfirio Diaz that cost perhaps a million or more lives and produced the reformist Constitution of 1917. Decades later the Cuban Revolution of 1959 brought a socialist government aligned with the Soviet Union, making the island a flashpoint of the Cold War. From the 1950s through the 1980s, that global rivalry drew the United States into interventions and into support for anti-communist regimes, while left-wing movements, some armed, pressed for change. Many countries fell under harsh military rule before democracy returned in the 1980s and early 1990s.

sections.heading: Key events and figures
sections.text: In Mexico, Francisco Madero, Emiliano Zapata (who demanded land under the banner 'Tierra y Libertad'), Pancho Villa, and Venustiano Carranza drove the revolution; the party that became the PRI then governed for most of the century. In Cuba, Fidel Castro and Che Guevara overthrew Fulgencio Batista in 1959, survived the Bay of Pigs invasion in 1961, and stood at the center of the Missile Crisis in 1962. A CIA-backed coup toppled Guatemala's Arbenz in 1954. Augusto Pinochet seized Chile on September 11, 1973, ending Salvador Allende's government; Argentina's junta waged a 'Dirty War' from 1976 to 1983; Brazil's military ruled from 1964 to 1985.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) When did the Mexican Revolution begin and end? 2) Which Mexican leader demanded land under 'Tierra y Libertad'? 3) Who did Castro overthrow in 1959? 4) Which 1962 crisis made Cuba a Cold War flashpoint? 5) Who overthrew Allende in Chile, and on what date? 6) During what years did Argentina's junta wage the Dirty War? Answers: 1) 1910 to 1920. 2) Emiliano Zapata. 3) Fulgencio Batista. 4) the Cuban Missile Crisis. 5) Augusto Pinochet, on September 11, 1973. 6) 1976 to 1983.

sections.heading: Common mistakes and exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: treating every leftist movement as identical, when they ranged from electoral parties to guerrilla groups with different aims. Mistake: ignoring outside intervention, when the Cold War drew powerful states deeply into the region's politics. Mistake: softening the dictatorships, which killed, tortured, and disappeared many thousands of people. Exit: (a) Which Mexican constitution came out of the revolution? (b) Roughly when did most of the region return to democracy? Answers: the Constitution of 1917; the 1980s and early 1990s.

lessons.title: Economy, society, culture, and modern Latin America
lessons.grammar_note: Remittances are the money that emigrants send home; for several countries they rival or exceed major exports as a source of income.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Describe the economic shifts of the late twentieth and early twenty-first centuries, the region's cultural achievements, the rise of Indigenous and Afro-Latin movements, and the patterns of migration that define Latin America today. Warm-up: can you name a Latin American writer or artist of global fame? By the end you should be able to connect economic cycles to social change, to appreciate the region's enormous cultural output, and to describe migration both within the region and beyond it, including the recent large movements of people seeking safety and opportunity.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: After the Second World War many countries pursued industrialization by substituting local manufactures for imports. The 1980s brought a severe debt crisis, often called the 'lost decade', followed in the 1990s by market-opening reforms and in the 2000s by a commodity boom that funded social spending under a wave of left-leaning governments sometimes called the 'pink tide'. Growth reduced poverty but left Latin America among the most unequal regions on earth, with large informal economies. Society urbanized dramatically, producing megacities such as Sao Paulo, Mexico City, Buenos Aires, Lima, and Bogota, while Indigenous and Afro-descendant communities pressed for recognition and rights.

sections.heading: Key events and figures
sections.text: Latin American culture reached the world through the literary 'Boom', with Gabriel Garcia Marquez, Jorge Luis Borges, Pablo Neruda, and Mario Vargas Llosa, and through Mexican muralists such as Diego Rivera and the painter Frida Kahlo; music from tango to samba and salsa spread widely. Indigenous movements gained new force: the Zapatistas rose in Chiapas in 1994, and Bolivia elected Evo Morales, its first Indigenous president, in 2006. Migration reshaped the region, with large emigration to the United States and Europe sending home remittances worth billions, and with major recent movements such as the departure of millions of Venezuelans after 2015 in search of safety and work.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) What did import substitution industrialization try to replace? 2) What is the 1980s crisis often called? 3) Name two authors of the literary 'Boom'. 4) What happened in Chiapas in 1994? 5) Who became Bolivia's first Indigenous president, and when? 6) What are remittances? Answers: 1) imported manufactured goods, with local production. 2) the 'lost decade'. 3) any two of Garcia Marquez, Borges, Neruda, Vargas Llosa. 4) the Zapatista uprising. 5) Evo Morales, in 2006. 6) money that emigrants send home to their families.

sections.heading: Common mistakes and exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: assuming economic growth automatically ended inequality, when Latin America remained highly unequal despite real gains. Mistake: treating the region's cultures as uniform, when Indigenous, African, European, and other roots blend differently from place to place. Mistake: picturing migration as only outward, when much movement is within the region, as with the recent Venezuelan exodus. Exit: (a) What name is given to the 2000s wave of left-leaning governments? (b) Name one Latin American megacity. Answers: the 'pink tide'; any of Sao Paulo, Mexico City, Buenos Aires, Lima, or Bogota.
